scqa: A lender approves 36-month personal loans by risk sub-grade. The loans from 2013–2014 made $71.7M of realized NPV.
What changed, and what it cost
The loans from 2015 lost $32.9M. Defaults rose from 12.3% in 2013 to 14.9%, and the mean interest rate fell from 13.4% to 11.3%. The business wants more approvals, but Risk accepts no more defaults.
Q: Can a new score approve more applicants at the current bad rate of 12.5%, and add money?

Yes. A scorecard approves 85.7% vs. 84.5% and adds $7.1M on the 2015 loans, and $5.1M or more under every cost assumption. Next step: a test on 10% of applications, together with a pricing test, because the price, not the cutoff, drove the 2015 loss.

method.h: Both policies run on the same 2015 applicants, and every number is an actual outcome
steps: Define the current policy on booked loans
The current policy approves the best sub-grades, up to about 85% of the 2015 applicants.
Use the declined group as the check group
The lender booked loans in the lowest sub-grades too. Each of these loans has a real outcome: default or no default, and the cash it returned.
Compare the two policies on actual outcomes
The scorecard approves the same number of applicants in a different order. The comparison uses the actual default rate and the realized NPV of the applicants that change sides.
notes: The scorecard learns from the loans of 2013–2014 and is tested on the loans of 2015, which it never saw.
Grade, sub-grade and interest rate are not inputs to the scorecard, because they are results of the lender's own policy.

The current policy is my assumption. The public data shows only booked loans, not the lender's approval rule. The result shows a method and the likely size of the gain. The test on 10% of applications measures the gain against the real policy.

scqa: An online merchant accepts card payments. A set of fixed rules approves, reviews or declines each transaction.
What changed, and what it cost

Fraud loss goes up. Stricter rules decline more good customers, and each false decline costs margin and goodwill. The analyst team can examine only 120 alerts each day, and fixed rules lose value as fraud patterns change.
Q: Which policy gives the lowest total cost of fraud loss, false declines and reviews, with the same review capacity?

A fraud score that puts each transaction in a tier by its expected cost in dollars. Total cost falls by $64,274 each month against the strongest current policy tested. It stops 71.2% of fraud dollars vs. 38.4%. Next step: a test on 10% of transactions.

projects.title: Which customers to send an email offer to
projects.result: Send the email to all customers and keep a 10% holdout. It earns $13k per campaign, with no targeting model.
projects.what: profit from an email to all customers, with no targeting model
projects.question: Which customers do we send the offer to, for the best return?
projects.answer: Send the men's email to all customers and keep a 10% holdout. It earns $13k per campaign of 100,000 customers.

pts: Spend effect against the no-email group: +$0.77 for each customer in 2 weeks (95% CI $0.49 to $1.05).
The three groups differ only by the email: the randomization check passes.
The men's email gives $10,362 more than the women's email for each campaign.

keyline.h: The extra margin is larger than the contact cost
pts: 30% margin on $0.77, less $0.10 for each email: $13,095 for each 100,000 customers (95% CI $4,554 to $21,635).
The email pays at any contact cost below $0.23.

keyline.h: A targeting model adds nothing at this cost
pts: At $0.10 an email, no targeting rule and no uplift model beats an email to all customers.
A shorter list (the top 25% by purchase history) pays only if the full contact cost is $0.25 or more.
A 10% holdout confirms each campaign and costs $1,309.

scqa: A retailer sent an email to customers who bought in the last year. Each customer went at random into one of three groups: the men's email, the women's email or no email. Visits, conversions and spend were measured for 2 weeks.
What changed, and what it cost
Each email has a contact cost. Most customers buy nothing in the test window, so the spend data is noisy, and the mean effect can hide customers where the email loses money.
Q: Which email version do we send, and to which customers, for the most incremental profit?
Send the men's email to all customers. Spend rises by $0.77 for each customer. Incremental profit: $13,095 for each campaign of 100,000 customers. Keep a 10% holdout.

c.s: The lever: all customers, or a targeted list
c.q: Does a targeted list beat an email to all customers?
c.ev: At $0.10 an email, no rule and no uplift model beats send-to-all. The top 25% by purchase history pays only at $0.25 or more.

c.q: Does the email pay at the assumed cost?
c.ev: It pays at any cost below $0.23 an email.
